questions.prompt: Explain the architectural and privacy advantages of on-device foundation models over cloud AI APIs in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains that user prompts and text remain entirely on-device without cloud network transmission.
Highlights low latency and full functionality while completely offline.
Notes that running local models incurs zero per-token or server subscription costs.

questions.modelAnswer: On-device foundation models provide complete data privacy because user prompts and text never leave the local Apple Silicon hardware. They eliminate network latency and continue functioning seamlessly even when the device is entirely offline. Furthermore, executing models on-device incurs zero per-token or cloud server API subscription costs for developers. When complex tasks exceed device capacity, requests can escalate to Private Cloud Compute without storing user data.

questions.prompt: Describe Private Cloud Compute and explain how it maintains user privacy in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains that Private Cloud Compute runs larger models on dedicated Apple Silicon servers for heavy queries.
Emphasizes that user data is processed statelessly and is never retained or stored in the cloud.
Mentions cryptographically verifiable software and independent security researcher auditability.

questions.modelAnswer: Private Cloud Compute handles complex AI queries that exceed on-device compute limits using dedicated Apple Silicon servers. It processes user requests statelessly, ensuring that data is never retained, logged, or accessible to Apple. The system uses cryptographic verification so the device only transmits requests to servers running publicly auditable code. This architecture extends the security and privacy of Apple devices directly into the cloud.

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of writingToolsBehavior and when developers should set it to .none in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains that writingToolsBehavior controls how system AI features like rewriting integrate with a text view.
Identifies that .none turns off Writing Tools completely for the target text container.
Provides examples of sensitive fields like passwords, security tokens, or code inputs needing .none.

questions.modelAnswer: The writingToolsBehavior property allows developers to control whether and how system Writing Tools interact with a text view. Setting the property to .none completely opts the text view out of AI proofreading, rewriting, and summarization. Developers should use .none on sensitive inputs like password fields, two-factor authentication tokens, and credit card inputs. It is also essential for code editors to prevent generative models from corrupting programming language syntax.

questions.prompt: Describe how to coordinate cloud synchronization during a Writing Tools session in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains implementing textViewWritingToolsWillBegin to pause background cloud sync and prevent merge conflicts.
Explains implementing textViewWritingToolsDidEnd to resume synchronization after AI text changes complete.

questions.modelAnswer: When a user begins an AI rewriting session, developers should implement textViewWritingToolsWillBegin in their text view delegate. This method pauses background synchronization engines, such as CloudKit or Core Data sync, to prevent concurrent data conflicts while the model modifies text. Once the user accepts or cancels the rewrite, the system invokes textViewWritingToolsDidEnd. The app then safely resumes cloud synchronization and persists the modified text content.

questions.prompt: Explain why machine learning inference must run asynchronously and describe how Swift concurrency helps in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains that synchronous inference blocks the main thread, causing frame drops and unresponsive UI.
Explains using async/await and Task to offload heavy computation to background threads smoothly.

questions.modelAnswer: Machine learning model inference and natural language processing require heavy computation on the Apple Neural Engine and GPU. Running inference synchronously on the main thread blocks UI event handling and produces noticeable frame drops. Swift concurrency solves this by allowing developers to define asynchronous methods using async and await. Offloading model processing into background tasks keeps animations fluid while streaming generated results back to the main actor.
